title: Find if Path Exists in Graph
description: Brute force to optimized: plain DFS/BFS from source versus Union-Find with path compression.

content.title: Find if Path Exists in Graph

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given n nodes labeled 0 to n-1, a list of undirected edges, and a source and destination node, return true if there is a valid path between source and destination.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","n, edges, source, destination"],["Output","true if source and destination are connected"],["Goal","Union every edge's endpoints; check if source and destination end up in the same connected component"],["Constraints","Up to 2*10^5 nodes and edges"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Is there any path between two nodes in an undirected graph?\"","A basic connectivity check, solvable directly via DFS/BFS, or efficiently via Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union) for repeated or large-scale connectivity queries"]]}

blocks.text: This is a direct connectivity query: source and destination are connected exactly when they belong to the same connected component of the graph. Union-Find is a natural fit, since processing every edge as a "union" operation directly groups nodes into their connected components, and checking whether two nodes share the same "representative" (root) answers the connectivity query in nearly constant time.

blocks.title: Analogy: Checking If Two People Belong to the Same Friend Group
blocks.text: Picture merging friend groups together every time two people are confirmed to know each other, then quickly checking if two specific people ended up in the exact same merged group, without needing to re-trace every individual connection each time.

blocks.caption: Union every edge's endpoints; source and destination are connected if they end up in the same set

blocks.text: Result: true (0-1-2 forms a connected triangle).
Result: false (nodes 0,1,2 form one component; 3,4,5 form a separate component).

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Every node starts as its own separate component (its own "parent" in a Union-Find structure).

Observation 2: Processing every edge as a UNION operation merges the two endpoints' components together, directly building up the graph's actual connected components.

Observation 3: After processing all edges, checking whether source and destination share the same ROOT (representative) in the Union-Find structure directly answers whether they are connected.

Observation 4: Using path compression (flattening the tree structure during FIND operations) keeps each operation nearly constant time, even for large numbers of nodes and edges.
This leads to a straightforward Union-Find: union every edge, then check if source and destination share the same root.
Perform a plain DFS or BFS starting from source, checking if destination is ever reached.
Why the code is written this way

items: A direct DFS/BFS from source correctly and efficiently answers a single connectivity query.

For this specific problem (one single query), DFS/BFS is already efficient; Union-Find is demonstrated here since it generalizes better to scenarios with many repeated connectivity queries on the same evolving graph.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n plus edges) for a single DFS/BFS query.
Space: O(n plus edges) for the adjacency list.
Limitation: for a single query, DFS/BFS is already efficient; Union-Find shines when connectivity must be checked repeatedly, or built incrementally as edges are added over time.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Initialize a parent array where every node starts as its own parent. Define find(x) to follow parent pointers to the root, applying path compression along the way. Define union(a, b) to find both roots and merge them if different. Process every edge as a union operation. Finally, return true if find(source) equals find(destination).
Use Union-Find with path compression: union every edge, then check if source and destination share the same root.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Union processed","Effect"],"rows":[["union(0,1)","merges components {0} and {1}"],["union(1,2)","merges {0,1} and {2}"],["union(2,0)","already in the same component, no change"],["find(0) vs find(2)","same root, connected"]]}

blocks.text: Processing every edge as a union operation correctly and progressively merges nodes into groups that exactly reflect the graph's true connected components; once all edges are processed, two nodes belong to the same connected component if and only if they share the same root in the Union-Find structure, which find(source) and find(destination) directly check, with path compression keeping every operation close to constant time.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O((n plus edges) times inverse Ackermann function), effectively linear.
Space: O(n) for the parent array.

items: Forgetting path compression in find(), which can degrade Union-Find to linear time per operation in the worst case.
Comparing parent[source] and parent[destination] directly instead of find(source) and find(destination), missing that a node's direct parent may not yet be the true root.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["source equals destination","Trivially true, a node is always connected to itself."],["No edges at all","True only if source equals destination."]]}

blocks.text: Explicitly stating "process every edge as a union, then check if source and destination share a root" demonstrates the Union-Find pattern clearly.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "check connectivity between two nodes, possibly with repeated queries", think: Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union) with path compression.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Plain DFS/BFS costs O(n plus edges) for a single query; Union-Find costs effectively linear time overall and generalizes better to repeated queries.

items: Pattern: Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union) with path compression.
Core Idea: union every edge's endpoints; two nodes are connected exactly when they share the same root.
Time: O(n plus edges) for DFS/BFS, effectively linear for Union-Find.
Space: O(n plus edges) for DFS/BFS, O(n) for Union-Find.
Most Important Observation: path compression keeps Union-Find operations nearly constant time.
Interview Difficulty: a foundational, easy Union-Find introduction problem.
One line memory trick: union every edge, then compare roots.
